title: Electrolysis of Aqueous Solutions
content:
# Electrolysis of Aqueous Solutions

## Learning Objectives

By the end of this lesson, you should be able to:
- Explain why aqueous electrolysis is more complex than molten electrolysis
- Predict the products at each electrode using the rules
- Write half-equations for aqueous electrolysis
- Describe the electrolysis of sodium chloride solution and copper sulfate solution

## Introduction

When an ionic compound is dissolved in water, the water provides additional ions (H⁺ and OH⁻). This makes predicting the products more complicated than for molten compounds.

## Key Concepts

### Why is Aqueous Electrolysis Different?

Water molecules partially dissociate:
$$\text{H}_2\text{O} \rightleftharpoons \text{H}^+ + \text{OH}^-$$

So in an aqueous solution, there are **four types of ions:**

| From the compound | From water |
|-------------------|------------|
| Metal cation (e.g., Na⁺) | H⁺ |
| Non-metal anion (e.g., Cl⁻) | OH⁻ |

**At each electrode, there is a choice of which ion is discharged.**

### Rules for Predicting Products

**At the cathode (choosing between metal ion and H⁺):**

| Metal reactivity | Product at cathode |
|------------------|--------------------|
| More reactive than hydrogen (K, Na, Li, Ca, Mg, Al) | **Hydrogen** |
| Less reactive than hydrogen (Zn, Fe, Cu, Ag) | **The metal** |

**Reason:** More reactive metals hold onto their electrons more tightly, so H⁺ is reduced instead.

**At the anode (choosing between non-metal ion and OH⁻):**

| Anion present | Product at anode |
|---------------|------------------|
| Halide ion (Cl⁻, Br⁻, I⁻) - concentrated | **The halogen** |
| Sulfate (SO₄²⁻), nitrate (NO₃⁻), or dilute halide | **Oxygen** (from OH⁻) |

**Reason:** Halide ions are easier to oxidise than OH⁻ when concentrated.

### Summary Table

| Cathode product | Anode product |
|-----------------|---------------|
| Hydrogen (if metal is reactive) OR Metal (if less reactive) | Halogen (if halide concentrated) OR Oxygen (otherwise) |

### Half-Equations for Aqueous Electrolysis

**At cathode (if hydrogen produced):**
$$\text{2H}^+ + 2\text{e}^- \rightarrow \text{H}_2$$

**At anode (if oxygen produced):**
$$\text{4OH}^- \rightarrow \text{O}_2 + \text{2H}_2\text{O} + 4\text{e}^-$$

### Example 1: Electrolysis of Sodium Chloride Solution (Brine)

**Ions present:** Na⁺, Cl⁻, H⁺, OH⁻

[DIAGRAM: Electrolysis of brine showing cathode producing H₂, anode producing Cl₂, with NaOH solution remaining]

**At cathode (-):**
- Choice: Na⁺ or H⁺
- Na is more reactive than H
- H⁺ is discharged
$$\text{2H}^+ + 2\text{e}^- \rightarrow \text{H}_2$$
Hydrogen gas produced (test: squeaky pop)

**At anode (+):**
- Choice: Cl⁻ or OH⁻
- Chloride is concentrated, so Cl⁻ is discharged
$$\text{2Cl}^- \rightarrow \text{Cl}_2 + 2\text{e}^-$$
Chlorine gas produced (test: bleaches litmus)

**What's left in solution:**
- Na⁺ and OH⁻ remain
- The solution becomes **sodium hydroxide (NaOH)**
- This is an important industrial process

**Products of brine electrolysis:**
1. Hydrogen (cathode)
2. Chlorine (anode)
3. Sodium hydroxide (solution)

### Example 2: Electrolysis of Dilute Sulfuric Acid

**Ions present:** H⁺, SO₄²⁻, OH⁻

**At cathode (-):**
$$\text{2H}^+ + 2\text{e}^- \rightarrow \text{H}_2$$
Hydrogen gas

**At anode (+):**
- Sulfate ions are very stable and hard to oxidise
- OH⁻ is discharged instead
$$\text{4OH}^- \rightarrow \text{O}_2 + \text{2H}_2\text{O} + 4\text{e}^-$$
Oxygen gas

**Overall:** Water is decomposed into hydrogen and oxygen
$$\text{2H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow \text{2H}_2 + \text{O}_2$$

### Example 3: Electrolysis of Copper Sulfate Solution

**Ions present:** Cu²⁺, SO₄²⁻, H⁺, OH⁻

**At cathode (-):**
- Choice: Cu²⁺ or H⁺
- Cu is less reactive than H
- Cu²⁺ is discharged
$$\text{Cu}^{2+} + 2\text{e}^- \rightarrow \text{Cu}$$
Copper metal deposited (pink/brown coating)

**At anode (+):**
- Sulfate is not discharged
- OH⁻ is discharged
$$\text{4OH}^- \rightarrow \text{O}_2 + \text{2H}_2\text{O} + 4\text{e}^-$$
Oxygen gas produced

**Observations:**
- Cathode gets coated with copper (pink/brown)
- Bubbles at anode (oxygen)
- Blue colour fades (Cu²⁺ ions removed)
- Solution becomes acidic (H⁺ and SO₄²⁻ left behind)

### Example 4: Electrolysis of Copper Sulfate with Copper Electrodes

**Special case:** When using copper (not inert) electrodes:

**At cathode (-):**
$$\text{Cu}^{2+} + 2\text{e}^- \rightarrow \text{Cu}$$
Copper deposited

**At anode (+):**
The copper anode itself dissolves:
$$\text{Cu} \rightarrow \text{Cu}^{2+} + 2\text{e}^-$$

**Result:** 
- Copper moves from anode to cathode
- Anode gets smaller, cathode gets bigger
- Solution concentration stays the same
- This is used for **purifying copper**

## Worked Examples

**Example 1:** Predict the products of electrolysing potassium bromide solution.

**Solution:**
Ions present: K⁺, Br⁻, H⁺, OH⁻

**At cathode:** K is more reactive than H, so H⁺ is discharged → **Hydrogen**

**At anode:** Bromide is a halide and is concentrated, so Br⁻ is discharged → **Bromine**

---

**Example 2:** Write the half-equations for the electrolysis of dilute sodium sulfate solution.

**Solution:**
Ions present: Na⁺, SO₄²⁻, H⁺, OH⁻

**At cathode:** Na is reactive, so H₂ forms
$$\text{2H}^+ + 2\text{e}^- \rightarrow \text{H}_2$$

**At anode:** Sulfate is stable, so O₂ forms
$$\text{4OH}^- \rightarrow \text{O}_2 + \text{2H}_2\text{O} + 4\text{e}^-$$

## Common Mistakes

- **Mistake:** Forgetting that water provides H⁺ and OH⁻ ions
- **Correct:** Always consider four ions in aqueous electrolysis

- **Mistake:** Always predicting the metal will form
- **Correct:** Reactive metals don't form - hydrogen is produced instead

- **Mistake:** Forgetting that halides give halogens (when concentrated)
- **Correct:** Concentrated Cl⁻, Br⁻, I⁻ → Cl₂, Br₂, I₂

## Practice Questions

1. Explain why the electrolysis of aqueous solutions is more complex than molten compounds. (2 marks)

2. Predict the products at each electrode for:
   a) Potassium iodide solution (2 marks)
   b) Copper chloride solution (2 marks)
   c) Dilute sodium hydroxide solution (2 marks)

3. Write the half-equations for the electrolysis of concentrated sodium chloride solution. (4 marks)

4. During the electrolysis of copper sulfate solution using carbon electrodes:
   a) State what you would observe at each electrode. (2 marks)
   b) Explain why the blue colour fades. (2 marks)

5. Explain why electrolysis of sodium chloride solution produces hydrogen, not sodium. (3 marks)

6. Describe and explain what happens when copper sulfate solution is electrolysed using copper electrodes. (4 marks)

## Key Terms Glossary

| Term | Definition |
|------|------------|
| Aqueous solution | A substance dissolved in water |
| Brine | Concentrated sodium chloride solution |
| Inert electrode | An electrode that doesn't react (e.g., carbon, platinum) |
| Discharge | When an ion gains or loses electrons at an electrode |

## Summary

- Aqueous solutions contain **four ions**: metal cation, non-metal anion, H⁺, OH⁻
- **At cathode:** Hydrogen if metal is reactive; metal if unreactive
- **At anode:** Halogen if halide concentrated; oxygen otherwise
- **Half-equations:**
  - Hydrogen: 2H⁺ + 2e⁻ → H₂
  - Oxygen: 4OH⁻ → O₂ + 2H₂O + 4e⁻
- **Brine electrolysis** produces: H₂, Cl₂, and NaOH
- **Copper electrodes** dissolve at anode and deposit at cathode (used for purification)
